inline.s: When I was eleven, I happened to see several traveling monks coming with a gourd and rain-hat slung over their shoulders. I asked my mother: 'What kind of people are these?' She said: 'They are wandering monks.' Inwardly I was pleased and watched them. The monks arrived, set down their loads against a tree, and asked after her and begged alms. My mother said: 'Please sit,' and quickly made tea and prepared a meal of alms, with great respect. When the meal was done, the monks rose, took up their loads, and raised one hand in thanks; my mother quickly avoided it, saying: 'Do not thank us.' The monks went straight off. I said: 'How rude the monks are, not to thank us for the meal.' My mother said: 'If they thanked us, there would be no blessing.' Inwardly I said: 'This is what makes a monk lofty,' and I pondered it earnestly. Thereupon I formed the resolve to leave the home life, but I was troubled that there was no convenient path. (Seen a seventh time by the mother.)

Fuzheng observes: suddenly offering a meal to monks, with not a trace left behind â€” such a great case; even the case of Zhaozhou testing the old woman at Taishan is no match for it. People know the merit of feeding monks to be a worldly blessing, but this mother and son rather attested the blessing of the Two-Footed Honored One.
The above closes the household case.
The thirty-sixth year, the cyclical year Dingsi

When I was twelve, living as I did I took no pleasure in the world, and when my father betrothed a wife for me I at once stopped it. One day I heard a monk from the capital say that the Venerable Xilin of the Bao'en Temple was a man of great virtue, and my heart at once longed to go to him. I told my father, who would not consent; I told my mother, who said: 'In raising a son one follows his will; only see that he accomplishes [his aim],' and so she sent me. That year, in the tenth month, I went to the temple, and the Grandmaster at first sight said, rejoicing: 'This child has an uncommon bone and spirit; if he were to be just a worldly monk, that would be a pity.' At the time the Great Master Wuji had just begun preaching in the Three-Master Hall of the temple. My grandfather took me there to call upon him, and just then Zhao Dazhou was present; at first sight he said, rejoicing: 'This child should be a teacher of men and gods.' Then he stroked me and asked: 'Do you love to be an official, or would you be a Buddha?' I answered at once: 'Be a Buddha.' Mr. Zhao said: 'This child must not be taken lightly; you should teach him well.' When I listened to the preaching, though I did not understand what was said, yet my mind felt a surging, as if there were something I knew but could not express. (Seen a second time by the father, an eighth time by the mother; and once each by the Venerable Xilin, the Great Master Wuji, and Zhao Dazhou. Dazhou, named Zhenji, styled Mengjing, was a man of Neijiang; he held office as Minister of Rites and Grand Secretary of the Wuying Hall, and was posthumously titled Wensu.)

Fuzheng reflects that had Patriarch Han not had this mother, he could not have left home, could not have carried his pure boy's body through to become a Buddha and patriarch; she was truly a Buddha's mother. Again, according to the Record of Buddhist Temples of Jinling: in the Jiajing era the abbot of the Bao'en Temple, Yongning, styled Xilin, kept a horse; whenever he went from the temple to the Ministry of Rites he rode it, and on mounting he would silently recite the Diamond and the Lotus Sutras; upon arriving at the ministry gate he dismounted and the recitation was done. Later, a woman who lived next to the temple was in childbirth, and that very night the horse died; the woman dreamed the horse entered her room and then bore a boy, exceedingly dull, who could only recite the two sutras aloud. Because of this he entered Xilin's temple as a monk, but he could not master any other sutra, and never came to know a single character. Hence the chronicle says the Master's [teacher] held the Diamond Sutra through life, never stopping from it at death.
The thirty-seventh year, the cyclical year Wuwu; the thirty-eighth year, Jiwei

When I was fourteen, the Grandmaster first chose from among his grandsons the learned and virtuous Master Jun to be my teacher. He first taught me the Lotus Sutra, and in three months I could recite it from memory. The other scriptures in circulation I had all already memorized. The Grandmaster said: 'This child is teachable; you must not miss the time with him,' and so he invited a noted teacher to instruct me. (The Great-grandmaster and Grandmaster are both the Venerable Xilin; seen a second time.)
The thirty-ninth year, the cyclical year Gengshen; the fortieth year, Xinyou; the forty-first year, Renxu

When I was seventeen, the Grandmaster again asked a tutor to teach me first the pursuit of the examinations. At the outset I read the Four Books together, then studied the Five Classics, the Masters, the Histories, the ancient prose, verse, and rhapsody. I could at once compose verse, and in the literary society made a rhapsody on the river, the piece 'On the River,' which the whole gathering at the time esteemed. Yet I was often ill, and so I began to wish to set aside the studies I had taken up. (Seen a third time by the Grandmaster.)
The forty-second year, the cyclical year Guihai; the forty-third year, Jiazi

When I was nineteen, because all my fellow students had succeeded, there were those who urged me to go for the examinations. At the time the Great Master Yungu, a man of the right Dharma-eye, dwelt in the mountains at Qixia; the Grandmaster had long supported him, and whenever he came and went always kept him to stay for days or a month. I served him very diligently and often heard his instruction. Just then Master Yungu came out of the mountains, and hearing there were those who urged me on, he feared I might have a mind to leave [the Way]. The Master earnestly opened to me the practice of leaving the world and entering meditation, and the wonder of awakening to the mind-ground. He enumerated the various patriarchs of the Transmission of the Lamp and the Lives of Eminent Monks, and bade me take them and read. I searched my book-satchel and found the Comprehensive Record of Zhongfeng; before I had finished the scroll I was greatly delighted and sighed: 'This is what my heart delights in.' Thereupon I resolved to do the work of leaving the world. I asked my grandfather to shear me, then burned and cast away all that I had studied, and gave my whole attention to a single matter of inquiry. Not yet grasping the essential, I set my mind single-mindedly on Buddha-recitation, day and night without ceasing. Before long, one night in a dream I saw Amitabha Buddha manifest and stand in the sky, where the sun was setting; I saw his face's light and auspicious marks, distinct and clear. I received his feet in worship, clinging with endless sorrow, and again wished to see the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteshvara and Mahasthamaprapta, who at once showed their half-bodies. From that time on the Three Sages were ever clearly before my eyes, and I gained confidence that the practice of cultivation could be accomplished. That year in winter the meditation hall of my temple built a practice-hall and invited the Great Master Wuji to preach the Prologue to the Avatamsaka. I thereupon received the full precepts from him and followed the lecture; when it reached the Ten Mystery Gates â€” 'the Sea-Seal's dense grove, the eternal dwelling place' â€” I suddenly awakened to the meaning of the dharma-realm's perfect and unhindered interpenetration. I earnestly admired the character of Qingliang [Chengguan], and so I named my own style Cheng-yin [Seal of Clarity]. I sought the Master's confirmation, and he said: 'Do you intend to enter this Dharma-gate?' He then spoke of Mount Qingliang, where in winter the ice piles hard and in summer snow still flies, and there is never heat, and that is why it is called Qingliang. From that time, whether walking or staying, the realm of ice and snow was ever before my eyes, and I vowed with all my heart to dwell there. In everything nothing pleased my heart, and the thought of leaving the world I never for a moment forgot. (Seen once by the Great Master Yungu, a second time by the Great Master Wuji, and a fourth time by the Grandmaster.)

Fuzheng's note: Patriarch Han's learning and letters were both already accomplished, and seeing the Buddha-Dharma in decline, he wished to take up the enterprise of [fulfilling] the spiritual and worldly dharma on one shoulder. Hence, at his friends' urging to take the examinations, he too conceived the desire to seize an official rank, so as to fulfill his own vow to spread the great Dharma. But the road of office is dangerous, and with the least carelessness one sinks into it. Fortunately he was warned by the Great Master Yungu, and so he devoted himself single-mindedly to the work of leaving the world, burned his study manuscripts, and begged the Grandmaster to shear him. The karmic occasion of his wholehearted practice and his resolve to awaken all began with Yungu. Yet there are those who single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name, year upon year, who still find it hard to see the Buddha â€” how could one so soon have the three Sages all manifest, so quickly answering his wish, and again and again have them clearly before his eyes? There are those who, at a practice-hall, listen to the teaching, take the precepts, and pursue inquiry, yet rely wholly on written words â€” who would attest their body, mind, and life? How could one, upon listening, have his whole body, mind, and life realized, seeing not a single word and phrase? Hearing the ten mystery gates of the Avatamsaka, he could at once awaken to the meaning of the dharma-realm's perfect, unhindered interpenetration, and could at once enter the Qingliang Dharma-gate, seeing ice and snow, and naming himself Cheng-yin. At that time the miraculous power of Wuji and the miraculous power of Patriarch Han were already in the inconceivable. Who would say that with words or without words, a great Dharma-master or a great Chan-master, there are two truths? One must know that one such as Patriarch Han is truly a man come from the West through many kalpas.
The forty-fourth year, the cyclical year Yichou

When I was twenty, on the sixteenth day of the first month, the Grandmaster entered his stilling. The previous year, on the last day [of the year], the Grandmaster gathered all his followers and said: 'I am eighty-three, and whether morning or evening I am going. I have taken on more than eighty disciples, and not one holds to my work.' Then he patted my back and said: 'This child I hoped might come to manhood, but now I cannot. Though he is young, yet he has the view of an older man. After my death, the great and small affairs of the house shall all be decided by him; do not discount them because he is young.' The assembly, choking back tears, received the charge. Seven days into the new year the Grandmaster put on his robes and went the round of the quarters, bidding farewell to each; the whole assembly was astonished. Three days later he spoke of his last affairs, showed a slight ailment, and refused to take medicine. He said: 'I am going; what use are drugs?' Then he gathered the assembly to recite the Buddha's name for five days and nights, holding the prayer-beads, with me held in his arms, and passed away serenely. Because the Grandmaster held the Diamond Sutra all his life, at the end he never stopped. The Grandmaster served as abbot of Bao'en for thirty years, dwelt in the abbacy, and on the eighteenth day of the third month after his passing, the abbacy caught fire, and the whole assembly marveled. That year, in the tenth month, the Great Master Yungu established a meditation session at Tianjie, gathering fifty-three renowned masters of the land to open the Dharma-gate of seated meditation. The Master strongly urged me to go and follow, and at that time the junior master consented, so I was able to take part. At first I did not know the key of applying the mind and suffered much from it. I offered incense and sought instruction, and the Master showed me how to examine earnestly the case of Buddha-recitation. From this I inquired, not swerving for a single thought. Within three months I was as in a dream; I saw not the assembly at all, nor knew that there were the affairs of daily life, so the whole assembly thought me resolute. Before many days had passed, because I used my mind too urgently, a swelling on my back broke out, very red and large; the Master was greatly concerned. I put on my kasaya and prayed with earnest grief before Weituo, saying: 'This must be an old enmity come to demand my life. I vow to recite the Avatamsaka Sutra ten times, and to borrow three months to finish this session, and afterwards will repay it.' Thus, when later in the night I was utterly weary, I went up to the meditation bed and slept deeply; I did not even know when the stilling ended, and when I rose, I had forgotten it. At dawn the Master asked how the ailment was; I said it was gone, and when he looked, it had already healed. The whole assembly was astonished; and so I finished a full session, and coming out I was as though I had never left the meditation seat: walking through the marketplace, I saw not a single person, and people all thought it strange. The founding of the Chan way south of the Yangtze began to flourish with the Great Master Yungu, but of the monks who dwelt in the temple practicing Chan, I alone [did so]. At the time the temple monks' robes all followed the lay fashion, much gaudy in color; I at that time cast aside all the clothes I had worn and sought only a patched robe to wear, and those who saw me thought it strange. (Seen a fifth time by the Grandmaster, once by the junior master, and a second time by the Great Master Yungu.)

Fuzheng observes: the Greatmaster Xilin of Xilin was by no means a common monk. He ended his long life in good fortune, knew his time beforehand, and got a grandson with an eye [of discernment], to whom he entrusted the affairs after death; and [the grandson] was able at last to requite the charge of patting his back, serving both worldly and spiritual dharma â€” rare indeed. Now everywhere there are meditation sessions, and those who enter to sit find only the comfort of a settled place for their pleasure; who knows the hardship of applying the mind? When Patriarch Han set his mind to Buddha-recitation, he early and often saw Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest with light. People content themselves with a little and are satisfied â€” who would again be willing to seek instruction and earnestly examine the case of Buddha-recitation? Patriarch Han once showed me, saying: 'If one recites the Buddha's name but will not put a death-defying mind to it, but only recites on floating thoughts, then in truth the habitual currents in the alaya-consciousness are entirely unseen; hence in Buddha-recitation one never sees the falling into place of a single thought. If Buddha-recitation is used powerfully, it even surpasses meditating on the cypress tree or a dry shit-stick.' The earnest examination of the case of Buddha-recitation has a basis. And so later when he traveled east and passed Jiahe, he came to Qizhen and paid respects at the stupa of the earlier Great Master Yungu, to make clear his Dharma-milk; and when he dwelt at Wuru, he established a six-period Buddha-recitation practice-hall in place of the meditation session. His prayer to Weituo to be rid of the back-swelling â€” how extraordinary was its efficacy! Were it not that in the three-month session he was as in a dream, seeing neither the assembly nor the affairs of daily life, and that leaving the meditation seat and walking the marketplace, he still saw no one as in sitting meditation â€” such earnest use of mind â€” one must not hope that praying to Weituo would bring such ease.
The forty-fifth year, the cyclical year Bingyin

When I was twenty-one, I came out from the meditation session. In the second month of that year, on the twenty-eighth day, at the hour of noon, the rain poured as from an overturned basin; suddenly a great thunderbolt came down from the stupa, fire broke out in the stupa hall, and in a moment the great hall was burned. By the Shen and You hours, the galleries and painted corridors of the various halls, more than a hundred and forty rooms, were all reduced to ashes. At the time my junior grandfather was abbot; when the matter was memorialized, an edict went down to the judicial office, and eighteen of those concerned in the matter were arrested together. The monks of the whole temple, fearing to be implicated, fled one after another; and there were no temple officers left with whom to consult. I stepped forward and did all I could to save them, personally carrying salt and vegetables to the prison to feed them. The distance from the temple to the Ministry of Justice was twenty li, and I traveled back and forth untiringly for three months; moreover I arranged protection in many ways, and the various parties to the affair finally escaped death. At the time Xuelang Gong, one year older than I, had taken refuge with the Great Master Wuji at the same time as I; we were very close to each other and were at the time regarded as brothers. I at once resolved with Gong on the intention to restore [the temple]. I also said: 'This is a great karmic occasion; it is not easy except for one with great good fortune and wisdom. You and I should throw our lives into practice, nourishing [our strength] to await the right time.' At that time I formed the resolve for a distant journey. Before long, the junior grandfather entered his stilling, and there was none to support the affairs of the great grandfather's household. Earlier, when the Grandmaster entered his stilling he had no savings, and the funeral expenses had all been borrowed, so there were many debts. When the households divided, I knew they could not be kept. Considering the Grandmaster's last charge, I contrived to repay all those borrowings in full; the remainder I divided among the disciples, each taking up his own work, and so the household was preserved. That year in the winter I followed the Great Master Wuji to hear the Lotus Sutra at the Tianjie Temple. Because I aimed at a distant journey, I kept examining the monks of the region to find one who could be my companion; after a long time I found none. One day I saw the rear shelf was spotless, and thought to myself that the keeper of the privy must be no common man; so I sought him out, and when I saw him he was merely a sallow, swollen, sick monk, which made me think him all the more extraordinary. Each morning when I rose, the work was already done, I did not know when he had swept. So I did not sleep, but secretly walked under the eaves to watch him; when the assembly was dismissed [from meditation], he had already finished tidying. Again, some days later I saw a place unclean and saw no one about; I asked the officers, who said: 'The privy keeper is sick in the guest room.' I went to check on him, and his condition was unbearable; I asked the master if he was at ease. He said: 'This karma-laden body is already hard to bear, and the sickness of craving is even harder to endure.' I asked why. He said: 'Whenever I see the alms-food served, I only wish I could let go of everything at once.' I laughed and said: 'This is only a long sickness longing for food,' and so I knew the man for real. I prepared some cakes and fruits and brought them in my sleeve to him, then asked his name. He said: 'Miaofeng,' and he was a man of Puzhou. I thereupon arranged to go abroad together with him. Some days later I looked for him again and did not see him; I knew in my heart that the man, fearing I might be a burden, had gone off secretly. (The junior grandfather, that is, the junior master; seen a second time. Xuelang Gong seen once, the Great Master Wuji a third time, and the privy keeper Miaofeng once.)
